name: Odds Ratio
description: Computes the odds ratio from a 2×2 table as the cross-product (a·d)/(b·c). It compares the odds of an outcome in the exposed group versus the unexposed group.
notes: An odds ratio of 1 means no association; above 1 suggests higher odds with exposure. Zero cells make it undefined or zero; the odds ratio overstates risk when the outcome is common.

name: Relative Risk
description: Computes the relative risk as the ratio of the incidence in the exposed group a/(a+b) to the incidence in the unexposed group c/(c+d). It shows how many times more likely the outcome is with exposure.
notes: A value of 1 means no difference in risk; above 1 means increased risk with exposure. Requires cohort or prospective data; the unexposed incidence must be nonzero.

name: Sensitivity
description: Computes the sensitivity (true positive rate) of a diagnostic test as true positives divided by all actually positive cases (true positives plus false negatives). It measures how well the test detects the condition.
notes: The result ranges from 0 to 1; high sensitivity means few missed cases (few false negatives). Sensitivity alone ignores false positives, so read it alongside specificity.

name: Specificity
description: Computes the specificity (true negative rate) of a diagnostic test as true negatives divided by all actually negative cases (true negatives plus false positives). It measures how well the test rules out the condition.
notes: The result ranges from 0 to 1; high specificity means few false alarms (few false positives). It complements sensitivity and should be interpreted together with it.

name: Prevalence
description: Computes prevalence as the number of diseased individuals divided by the total population size. It gives the proportion of a population that has the condition at a given time.
notes: The result is a fraction between 0 and 1; multiply by 100 for a percentage. Prevalence reflects existing cases, unlike incidence which counts new cases over time.

name: Precision (PPV)
description: Computes precision, or positive predictive value, as true positives divided by all predicted positives (true positives plus false positives). It gives the fraction of positive predictions that are correct.
notes: The result ranges from 0 to 1. Precision depends on prevalence, so a highly accurate test can still have low PPV when the condition is rare.

name: Negative Predictive Value
description: Computes the negative predictive value as true negatives divided by all predicted negatives (true negatives plus false negatives). It gives the fraction of negative predictions that are correct.
notes: The result ranges from 0 to 1 and, like PPV, depends on prevalence. A high NPV means a negative result is trustworthy for ruling out the condition.

name: Youden's J Index
description: Computes Youden's J index as sensitivity plus specificity minus 1, summarizing a diagnostic test's overall performance in a single number. It represents the maximum vertical distance from the ROC diagonal.
notes: The index ranges from 0 (useless) to 1 (perfect); it can be negative for a worse-than-chance test. It weights sensitivity and specificity equally regardless of prevalence.

name: Positive Likelihood Ratio
description: Computes the positive likelihood ratio as sensitivity divided by (1 minus specificity), i.e. the true positive rate over the false positive rate. It shows how much a positive test result raises the odds of disease.
notes: Values above 1 increase, and above 10 strongly increase, the probability of disease. The denominator (1 minus specificity) must be nonzero; a perfect specificity makes it undefined.

name: Number Needed to Treat
description: Computes the number needed to treat as the reciprocal of the absolute risk reduction (control event rate minus experimental event rate). It estimates how many patients must be treated to prevent one additional bad outcome.
notes: Enter event rates as decimals; the two rates must differ, and the control rate should exceed the experimental rate for a beneficial treatment. Round the result up to a whole number of patients.

name: Attributable Risk (Risk Difference)
description: Gives the attributable risk (risk difference), computed as p1-p2 from the risk p1 in the exposed group and p2 in the unexposed group. It is the excess disease risk attributable to the exposure.
notes: p1 and p2 are probabilities between 0 and 1. A positive result indicates increased risk from exposure and a negative result a protective effect; it is an absolute, not relative, measure.

name: Basic Reproduction Number (beta·c·D)
description: Computes the basic reproduction number R0 as the product of the transmission probability per contact, the contact rate, and the duration of infectiousness. It gives the average number of secondary infections one case causes in a fully susceptible population.
notes: The contact rate (per day) and duration (days) must use consistent time units so R0 is dimensionless. It assumes a homogeneously mixing, entirely susceptible population; real outbreaks reduce this to an effective value.

name: Basic Reproduction Number (SIR Model)
description: Derives the basic reproduction number in the SIR model as the transmission rate divided by the recovery rate. It represents the expected number of new infections generated by one infectious individual before recovery in a susceptible population.
notes: Beta and gamma must share the same time unit (per day) so the ratio is dimensionless. The recovery rate gamma equals one over the mean infectious period; R0 above 1 predicts epidemic growth.

name: Effective Reproduction Number (R0·S)
description: Calculates the effective reproduction number by multiplying the basic reproduction number R0 by the susceptible fraction of the population. It gives the actual average number of secondary cases when part of the population is already immune.
notes: The susceptible fraction S is a proportion between 0 and 1, not a percentage. When the effective number falls below 1 the epidemic declines; this drop reflects depleted or vaccinated susceptibles.

name: Herd Immunity Threshold
description: Computes the herd immunity threshold as one minus the reciprocal of R0, giving the fraction of the population that must be immune to halt sustained transmission. Above this fraction the effective reproduction number drops below one.
notes: Valid only for R0 greater than 1, and expresses a proportion between 0 and 1. It assumes random mixing and uniform immunity; heterogeneous contact patterns can raise or lower the real threshold.

name: Reproduction Number from Growth Rate
description: Estimates the reproduction number from the exponential epidemic growth rate and the generation time using R = exp(r·Tc), assuming a fixed generation interval. It links the observed speed of spread to per-generation transmission.
notes: The growth rate (per day) and generation time (days) must use matching time units. This exponential approximation assumes a delta-distributed generation time; a variable interval requires the moment-generating form and lowers the estimate.

name: Epidemic Doubling Time
description: Calculates the time for the number of cases to double during exponential growth, as the natural log of 2 divided by the growth rate. A shorter doubling time signals faster epidemic spread.
notes: The growth rate must be positive and its unit sets the result unit (per day gives days). It applies only during genuine exponential growth; once growth slows the doubling time is no longer constant.

name: Force of Infection
description: Computes the force of infection, the per-capita rate at which susceptible individuals become infected, as the transmission coefficient times the infectious fraction I over N. It is the instantaneous hazard of acquiring infection.
notes: I and N must be counts in the same population so I/N is a proportion; the result carries the time unit of beta (per day). It assumes frequency-dependent, homogeneous mixing.

name: Attack Rate
description: Calculates the attack rate as the number of new cases divided by the population at risk over a defined outbreak period. It is the cumulative proportion of an exposed group that develops the disease.
notes: Both counts must cover the same at-risk group and time window; the result is a proportion between 0 and 1. Despite the name it is a risk, not a true rate with a time denominator.

name: Incidence Rate (Person-Time)
description: Computes the incidence rate as new cases divided by the total person-time at risk. Unlike a simple proportion, it accounts for varying follow-up durations and yields a rate per unit person-time.
notes: Person-time (person-years here) sets the denominator unit, so the result is per person-year. Each individual contributes time only while at risk; time after diagnosis or loss to follow-up must be excluded.

name: Cumulative Incidence (Risk)
description: Calculates cumulative incidence, the proportion of an initially at-risk group that develops the disease over a follow-up period, as new cases divided by the number at risk. It estimates the average individual risk.
notes: The number at risk is measured at baseline; the result is a proportion between 0 and 1 tied to a fixed follow-up period. It assumes little loss to follow-up, otherwise incidence rate methods are preferred.

name: Incidence from Prevalence and Duration
description: Estimates incidence rate from prevalence and mean disease duration using I = P / ((1-P)·D), derived from the steady-state relationship prevalence odds equals incidence times duration. It infers how fast new cases arise from cross-sectional data.
notes: Prevalence P is a proportion between 0 and 1; the result unit is the reciprocal of the duration unit (per year here). It holds only in a steady state with stable incidence and duration.

name: Positive Predictive Value (Bayes)
description: Computes the positive predictive value via Bayes' theorem: the probability that a person with a positive test truly has the disease, from sensitivity, specificity, and pretest prevalence. It answers how much a positive result should be trusted.
notes: Sensitivity, specificity, and prevalence are all proportions between 0 and 1. PPV depends strongly on prevalence, falling sharply when disease is rare even with an accurate test.

name: Negative Predictive Value (Bayes)
description: Computes the negative predictive value via Bayes' theorem: the probability that a person with a negative test is truly disease-free, from sensitivity, specificity, and pretest prevalence. It quantifies how reassuring a negative result is.
notes: All three inputs are proportions between 0 and 1. NPV rises as prevalence falls, so a negative test is most reassuring for uncommon conditions; it drops when disease is common.

name: Diagnostic Odds Ratio
description: Calculates the diagnostic odds ratio, a single measure of test discrimination, as (Se·Sp)/((1-Se)·(1-Sp)). It is the ratio of the odds of a positive result in diseased versus non-diseased individuals.
notes: Sensitivity and specificity are proportions between 0 and 1; the result is dimensionless and ranges from 0 upward, with 1 meaning no discrimination. It is undefined when sensitivity or specificity equals 1.

name: Negative Likelihood Ratio
description: Computes the negative likelihood ratio as (1 - sensitivity) divided by specificity. It expresses how much a negative test result lowers the odds of disease, feeding into Bayesian post-test probability.
notes: Sensitivity and specificity are proportions between 0 and 1; the result is dimensionless. Values well below 1 (near 0.1) strongly rule out disease, while values near 1 change probability little.

name: False Positive Rate
description: Computes the false positive rate as one minus specificity, the proportion of disease-free individuals who nonetheless test positive. It equals the probability of a positive result given no disease.
notes: Specificity is a proportion between 0 and 1, and so is the result. This is the type I error of the test; it does not by itself indicate how many positives are false, which depends on prevalence.

name: False Negative Rate
description: Computes the false negative rate as one minus sensitivity, the proportion of truly diseased individuals who test negative. It equals the probability of a negative result given disease is present.
notes: Sensitivity is a proportion between 0 and 1, and so is the result. This is the type II error (missed cases); a low value is essential when failing to detect disease is dangerous.

name: Youden's J Statistic
description: Computes Youden's J as sensitivity plus specificity minus one, summarizing a test's overall ability to distinguish diseased from healthy in a single number. It is often used to choose an optimal cutoff.
notes: Sensitivity and specificity are proportions between 0 and 1; J ranges from 0 (useless) to 1 (perfect). It weights sensitivity and specificity equally, which may not suit unequal costs of the two errors.

name: Post-Test Odds
description: Calculates post-test odds by multiplying the pretest odds of disease by the likelihood ratio of the test result. It is the core step of Bayesian diagnostic reasoning, updating belief after a test.
notes: Both odds and likelihood ratio are dimensionless. Inputs must be odds, not probabilities; convert a pretest probability p to odds as p/(1-p) first, and convert the result back to probability if needed.

name: Post-Test Probability from Odds
description: Converts post-test odds back into a probability using O/(1+O). It turns the odds produced by Bayesian updating into the intuitive probability that disease is present after the test.
notes: The input must be odds (0 upward), not a probability; the result is a probability between 0 and 1. Applying it to a value already expressed as a probability gives a meaningless number.

name: Attributable Risk Percent (Exposed)
description: Computes the attributable risk percent among the exposed as (RR-1)/RR, the fraction of disease risk in exposed individuals that is due to the exposure. It estimates the proportion of cases preventable by removing the exposure.
notes: Relative risk must exceed 1 for a positive, meaningful fraction; the result is a proportion between 0 and 1. It assumes RR reflects a causal effect free of confounding.

name: Population Attributable Risk
description: Calculates population attributable risk as the incidence in the total population minus the incidence in the unexposed. It is the excess disease occurrence in the whole population attributable to the exposure.
notes: Both incidences must be on the same scale (proportions or rates); the result inherits that scale. It reflects both the exposure's effect and how common the exposure is in the population.

name: Population Attributable Fraction
description: Computes the population attributable fraction from the proportion exposed and the relative risk using Pe(RR-1)/(1+Pe(RR-1)). It gives the share of total disease in the population that could be prevented by eliminating the exposure.
notes: Proportion exposed is between 0 and 1 and RR should exceed 1; the result is a proportion between 0 and 1. It assumes a causal, unconfounded relative risk applying uniformly across the population.

name: Number Needed to Harm
description: Computes the number needed to harm as the reciprocal of the absolute risk increase. It is the number of people who must be exposed or treated for one additional adverse outcome to occur.
notes: Absolute risk increase is a proportion between 0 and 1; the result is a count of people. A smaller NNH means a more harmful exposure; it is undefined when there is no risk increase.

name: Case Fatality Rate
description: Calculates the case fatality rate as the number of deaths divided by the number of diagnosed cases of a disease. It measures the proportion of people with the disease who die from it.
notes: Both are counts over the same case group and period; the result is a proportion between 0 and 1. It depends heavily on case ascertainment, so undercounting mild cases inflates it.

name: Crude Mortality Rate (per 1000)
description: Computes the crude mortality rate as deaths divided by population, scaled per 1000 people, over a given period. It gives overall deaths per 1000 without adjusting for age or other structure.
notes: Deaths and population must cover the same period and area; the result is per 1000. Being crude, it is confounded by the population's age structure and should not be compared directly across dissimilar populations.

name: Standardized Mortality Ratio
description: Calculates the standardized mortality ratio as observed deaths divided by expected deaths, where expected deaths come from applying a reference population's rates. A value above 1 means more deaths than expected.
notes: Both are counts; the result is dimensionless. Expected deaths must be derived from an appropriate age-standardized reference; SMRs from different standards are not directly comparable.

name: Vaccine Efficacy (1 - RR)
description: Computes vaccine efficacy as one minus the relative risk of disease in vaccinated versus unvaccinated people. It is the proportional reduction in disease risk attributable to vaccination.
notes: Relative risk is a proportion typically below 1 for a protective vaccine; the result is a fraction (multiply by 100 for percent). A negative value would imply the vaccine increased risk.

name: Vaccine Efficacy (Incidence)
description: Calculates vaccine efficacy from incidence as (Iu - Iv)/Iu, the relative reduction in disease incidence between unvaccinated and vaccinated groups. It measures the protective effect observed in a trial or cohort.
notes: Both incidences must be on the same scale over comparable follow-up; the result is a fraction (times 100 for percent). It equals 1 minus the incidence ratio and assumes comparable exposure between groups.

name: Directly Age-Standardised Rate

variables.label: Standard population in each age group

description: Weights age-specific rates by a standard population so populations with different age structures can be compared.
notes: WHO and the European Standard Population are common standards.

name: Incidence Rate Ratio
description: Compares incidence rates between exposed and unexposed person-time.
notes: Used in cohort studies with differing follow-up.

name: Kaplan–Meier Survival Probability

variables.label: Number at risk just before each event time

description: Gives the product-limit estimate of survival after a series of event times, allowing for censored patients (Kaplan and Meier 1958).
notes: Those censored leave the risk set without counting as deaths.

name: Hazard Ratio from Median Survival Times
description: Approximates the hazard ratio from two median survival times, assuming exponential survival.
notes: Below 1 favours the treatment.

name: Relative Risk Reduction
description: Gives the proportional reduction in risk from a treatment.
notes: Often sounds impressive; also report the absolute reduction and NNT.

name: Epidemic Final Size (SIR Model)
description: Gives the fraction of a population eventually infected in a simple SIR epidemic, solving z = 1 − e^(−R₀z).
notes: R₀ = 2 infects about 80 %, well beyond the 50 % herd-immunity threshold.

name: Peak Prevalence in an SIR Epidemic
description: Gives the largest share of the population infected at the same time in a simple SIR epidemic that starts with almost everyone susceptible.
notes: Flattening the curve lowers this peak.

name: Vaccine Coverage Needed for Herd Immunity
description: Gives the share of the population to vaccinate to stop sustained spread, allowing for imperfect vaccine effectiveness.
notes: Measles (R₀ 12–18) needs about 95 % coverage.

name: Secondary Attack Rate
description: Gives the share of exposed susceptible contacts who become infected, a measure of transmissibility in households or settings.
notes: Excludes the primary case from both counts.

name: Years of Potential Life Lost
description: Adds up years lost by deaths before a reference age (often 65 or 75), emphasising premature deaths.
notes: Deaths after the reference age count zero.

name: Disability-Adjusted Life Years (DALY)

variables.label: Standard life expectancy at death age

description: Gives the disease burden as years of life lost to early death plus years lived with disability (WHO Global Burden of Disease).
notes: One DALY is one lost year of healthy life.

name: Quality-Adjusted Life Years (QALY)
description: Weights each period of life by its quality (1 = full health, 0 = death) and adds them up.
notes: Used in cost-effectiveness analysis by NICE and others.

name: Incremental Cost-Effectiveness Ratio (ICER)
description: Gives the extra cost per extra unit of health gained by a new intervention.
notes: Compared with willingness-to-pay thresholds such as £20,000–30,000 per QALY (NICE).

name: Infant Mortality Rate
description: Gives deaths of infants under one year per 1000 live births, a key indicator of population health.
notes: Ranges from about 2 to over 50 across countries.

name: Maternal Mortality Ratio
description: Gives maternal deaths per 100,000 live births (WHO definition: during pregnancy or within 42 days after).
notes: The UN target is below 70 globally by 2030.

name: Total Fertility Rate
description: Gives the average number of children a woman would have at current age-specific birth rates.
notes: About 2.1 is replacement level.

name: Rate of Natural Increase
description: Gives the population growth per 1000 people from births minus deaths, excluding migration.
notes: Divide by 10 for percent.

name: Excess Mortality P-Score
description: Gives excess deaths as a percentage of the expected number, used to compare crises across countries.
notes: Expected deaths come from pre-crisis years.

name: Screening Yield
description: Gives the expected number of true cases a screening programme will detect.
notes: Add false positives nn(1 − pr)(1 − specificity) to plan follow-up capacity.

name: False Positives in Screening
description: Gives the expected number of healthy people wrongly flagged by a screening test.
notes: At low prevalence false positives can outnumber true cases.

name: Standardised Incidence Ratio 95 % Confidence Interval (Upper)
description: Gives the exact upper 95 % confidence limit of an SIR or SMR from the observed count.
notes: The lower limit uses chi2inv(0.025, 2o)/2/E.

name: Number Needed to Screen
description: Gives how many people must be screened over a period to prevent one death.
notes: The screening counterpart of the number needed to treat.

name: Case–Control Odds Ratio (Matched Pairs)

variables.label: Pairs with case exposed, control not
Pairs with control exposed, case not

description: Gives the odds ratio for a matched case–control study from the discordant pairs only.
notes: Concordant pairs carry no information.

name: 8-Hour Time-Weighted Average Exposure
description: Gives a worker's average exposure over an 8-hour shift, compared with the occupational exposure limit (TWA).
notes: Unmeasured time counts as zero exposure only if truly unexposed.

name: Exposure Index for a Mixture
description: Adds the ratios of each chemical's exposure to its limit for substances with similar effects; above 1 exceeds the combined limit.
notes: Assumes additive effects.

name: Dilution Ventilation Rate
description: Gives the fresh-air flow needed to keep a contaminant generated at a steady rate below a target concentration.
notes: K allows for incomplete mixing.

name: NIOSH Recommended Weight Limit

variables.label: Vertical height of hands at origin

description: Gives the load nearly all healthy workers can lift without raised risk of back injury, from the revised NIOSH lifting equation (1991).
notes: Look up the frequency and coupling multipliers in the NIOSH tables.

name: NIOSH Lifting Index
description: Compares the actual load with the recommended weight limit; above 1 increases risk, above 3 most workers are at risk.
notes: Redesign the task rather than select stronger workers.

name: Daily Vibration Exposure A(8)
description: Normalises hand-arm or whole-body vibration exposure to an 8-hour day (EU Directive 2002/44/EC).
notes: Hand-arm action value 2.5, limit 5 m/s².
